note: A perk is a fact about the PC, so it is pure benefit and there is one per run (perks-and-quirks.md section 1). SPEC section 6.1 unlocks exactly one at game start; section 14.3's meta-progression adds the rest. Adding an entry here adds it to the offered list, and the code knows only how to apply the modifier ids it finds - a perk names a knob and never adds a number.

entries.name: It's my first day
entries.blurb: The court is inclined to make allowances, this once.

entries.name: Righteous
entries.blurb: The Church has decided, on balance, to be pleased with you.
entries.note: Clergy gain loyalty every turn (section 3). You get more out of them without giving as much - and since a contented clergyman is a standing weight against rebel sentiment at high prominence, this is quietly a sentiment perk as much as a charity one. A drift term on one class of contact: a knob that already exists, turned.

entries.name: Good first impression
entries.blurb: People tend to like you before they know why.
entries.note: Every new contact starts warmer: governors of founded towns, patrons arriving, the commander who comes with the Marshal's troops, the clergyman of a new church. Strongest for a player who goes wide and long - a colony of nine towns has met a great many people; one holding two for six years has met almost nobody. That variance is SPEC section 14.3's variety rather than power. It does not touch the Crown's officers, who are fixed in every run and whose loyalties are characterisation.

entries.name: Read between the lines
entries.blurb: You have a good ear for what a man is not saying.
entries.note: Contacts' perception leans are reduced when reporting to you. They still deceive themselves - the Marshal still minimises every threat, the clergy still sees the worst - but they present it to you more plainly. The only perk that changes what you can SEE rather than what you can do, and the one that rewards a player who reads letters closely rather than one who plays the numbers.

entries.name: Good PR
entries.blurb: The pamphlets are unusually kind to you.
entries.note: Your optics all land in your favour - good ones ring harder, bad ones ring quieter (prestige.md section 4). It does NOT make an optic decay; nothing does. It scales what each is worth in the tally, so a run with two rebellions in it is still a run with two rebellions in it, and merely less ruinous. That is the difference between a perk and a pardon.

entries.name: My boss is a jerk
entries.blurb: Everyone knows whose treasury said no.
entries.note: When the CROWN breaks your promise it costs you far less loyalty. REFUSING (crown-standing.md section 3) breaks every gold promise at once, and because the PC typically owes several people it lands as a broad collapse in goodwill rather than one penalty - then worse compliance, then rising sentiment. This perk defuses the nastiest spiral in the game, and only ever matters once you are already in trouble. A promise you broke yourself costs exactly what it always did.

entries.name: Well connected at court
entries.blurb: A word from you goes further than it has any right to.
entries.note: Granting a Crown officer's demand earns more loyalty than it should. The gold leaves your accounts exactly as it would have; what you buy with it is worth more, which makes the officers cheaper to keep and the Squeeze's 'more hands out' dimension less punishing. It turns what a deed is WORTH and never the promise, the payment or the Crown's books.

entries.name: Hard to say no to
entries.blurb: People find it difficult to disappoint you.
entries.note: Your urging weighs more in a governor's intent deliberation (governor-objectives.md section 4). Worth knowing what this does NOT do: it never overrides him. crown_urging remains one of eight considerations against his own reading of his town, so this wins close arguments and loses hopeless ones. The Crown's pressure, not the Crown's command. Because a fresh urging is already at the ceiling, what it really buys is that the letter is still scoring next spring when an ordinary one has faded.
